newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European centre for missing children launched.
newsitem.headline: European centre for missing children launched.

text.p: A European Centre for Missing and Exploited Children was launched on Thursday in Belgium, a country still reeling from the discovery of paedophile murderers in its midst.

Modelled on a similar U.S. organisation, the centre hopes to cooperate with judicial authorities in the hunt for missing children and monitor the whereabouts of known sex offenders, chairman Daniel Cardon de Lichtbuer told a news conference.

In time, the centre should foster the creation of a pan-European network of similar organisations. At present, only Britain has a privately run missing persons bureau, but this is not focused exclusively on children, officials said.

"It's European because the problem is European," Lichtbuer said, referring to the recent exposure of a paedophile ring in France. "One year ago Belgium believed it was only here that nothing was right. Since, we have seen the problem has a wider dimension."

Horror in Belgium at the discovery last August of the bodies of four murdered, sexually abused children and the rescue of two others in a state of near starvation turned to disgust when an inquiry concluded they could probably have been saved if the justice system had functioned properly.

The chief suspect in the murder case, Marc Dutroux, who has been in detention since last August, was a previously convicted sex offender who was released from prison in 1992 after serving just two years of a 13-year sentence for raping five children.
Another previously convicted child molester was arrested separately this year in connection with the 1992 murder of a nine-year-old girl in Brussels.
The new centre will have a telephone hotline to receive information about missing children and computer software to store and adjust their photographs to reflect the passage of time.
The centre also wants to establish, in cooperation with the police, a database of convicted child sex offendors.

Lichtbuer said, however, the centre would have limits. "We must never compete with the law, or carry out dual inquiries. We have to aid institutions of the state, not replace them," Lichtbuer said, appealing for the Centre to be given time to demonstrate its worth.
Parents of the children whose bodies were found last year have refused so far to endorse the centre.
Lichtbuer's appointment has also been criticised because of his background as a senior Belgian banker.
